opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are some really interesting parallels and also some important differences. One lesson from self-driving is that getting a demo working is very different from getting something reliable enough to deploy. The long tail of edge cases is brutal, and the last few percent of reliability can take years.

That said, I'm actually somewhat optimistic that robotics might be easier in some ways. With self-driving, you basically need near-perfect reliability before you can deploy, because mistakes can be catastrophic and people's lives are at stake. In a lot of robotic manipulation settings, if a robot drops a shirt while folding laundry, or fumbles picking an item off a shelf, it can just try again. The cost of failure is much lower, so you can get into the world earlier with a system that's 90 or 95 percent good, and then use the data from real deployment to keep improving.

On the other hand, robotics is harder in other ways. Driving is, in a sense, one task: you have a fairly well-defined action space, steering and acceleration, and the environment is structured with roads, lanes, and rules. In robotics we want robots to do a huge range of tasks in very unstructured environments, homes, warehouses, kitchens, with contact-rich manipulation of deformable objects and lots of variability. The breadth of the problem is much bigger.

There's also the data question. Self-driving companies could put cameras on cars people were already driving and collect huge amounts of data. Robotics doesn't have that natural fleet yet, so a big part of the challenge is figuring out how to scale data collection, whether through teleoperation, learning from human video, simulation, or deploying robots that are useful enough to generate their own data.

So my take is that we shouldn't assume robotics will follow the same timeline as self-driving. The lower stakes of failure could let us deploy sooner and build a data flywheel, but the generality we're aiming for means we need models that really generalize, which is why I'm excited about foundation-model approaches for robots.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts driving’s simple steering and acceleration controls with robotics’ broad task range, but it does not clearly identify a higher-dimensional control space as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It describes robotics as spanning unstructured, variable environments; it does not say commercial robotics can be viable within a narrower distribution of operating scenarios than self-driving.

r003.rationale: It says self-driving mistakes can be catastrophic and threaten lives, while many robot failures are low-cost and allow the robot to try again.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because self-driving is really the one example we have of a robot that's been deployed at scale in the real world, so it's a natural reference point. And there are definitely similarities. In both cases you have a physical system acting in an unstructured environment, you have a long tail of situations you need to handle, and the cost of a mistake is real, it's not like a chatbot where you just regenerate the response.

But I actually think the differences are more interesting than the similarities. The first is the task. In self-driving, there's essentially one task: get from point A to point B without hitting anything, while following the rules of the road. It's an incredibly hard task, but it's a single, well-defined objective, and you can pour a decade of engineering into that one problem. With general-purpose robots, the whole point is the breadth. You want a robot that can fold laundry, and load a dishwasher, and bus a table, and the set of things people want is essentially open-ended. So you can't hand-engineer your way through each task the way you could with driving. That's actually why I think learning, and especially foundation models, matter so much more for robotics than they did historically for self-driving.

The second difference is the tolerance for failure. If a car makes a mistake at sixty miles an hour, someone can die. That means the bar you have to clear before you can deploy anything is extraordinarily high, and you basically have to be near-perfect before you get any real-world signal. In a lot of robot manipulation settings, the consequences of a mistake are much lower. If a robot drops a shirt or misplaces a cup, that's annoying, but it's recoverable. And I think that's actually a huge advantage for robotics, because it means you can deploy earlier, with a system that's maybe eighty or ninety percent reliable, and then learn from the failures. That flywheel of deployment and data collection is something self-driving had to wait a very long time to get going.

The flip side is that the data problem is harder for us. Self-driving had this very natural data source: millions of people driving cars every day, and you could instrument those cars and collect data at scale. Nobody is out there teleoperating robots through their chores. So we've had to be much more deliberate about how we get data, whether that's teleoperation, or cross-embodiment data from lots of different robots, or leveraging video and language from the internet. And the hardware itself is still far less standardized than a car, which makes everything from data to deployment a little more fragmented.

So if I had to summarize: self-driving is a narrow, high-stakes problem where the challenge was getting to near-perfect reliability on one task. Robotics is a broad, often lower-stakes problem where the challenge is generality and data. I actually think the second one is more tractable than people assume, precisely because you don't have to be perfect on day one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics’ broader range of tasks, but does not identify a higher-dimensional control space as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It contrasts self-driving’s single task with robotics’ open-ended breadth; it does not say commercial robotics can succeed within a narrower distribution of operating scenarios.

r003.rationale: It says mistakes in robot manipulation, such as dropping a shirt or misplacing a cup, are lower consequence and recoverable compared with mistakes by a car, making earlier deployment an advantage.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is both harder and easier in different ways. Self-driving has a relatively well-defined task: get from point A to point B safely. But the reliability requirement is incredibly high, and you don’t get to control all the situations the car encounters. You have to handle the world as it is, including some very unusual events.

With robotics, you have more flexibility in choosing the first application. You can pick a task and an environment where a mistake is recoverable. If a robot misses a grasp, it can try again. That gives you a path to delivering value before you’ve solved every possible edge case.

The harder part is the breadth of what we want robots to do. Manipulating different objects, dealing with contact, and adapting to different homes or workplaces are all challenging. And we don’t have the same abundance of data. You can collect driving data while people drive, but collecting useful robot interaction data generally requires operating the robot.

So I think the commercial question is: can you find applications where the robot is useful at its current level of capability, and then use that deployment to learn and improve? You don’t necessarily need a robot that can do everything to build a useful business.

r001.rationale: The response cites task breadth, manipulation, contact, and limited data as challenges, but does not identify higher-dimensional control as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says robotics can start with a chosen task and environment where mistakes are recoverable, while self-driving must handle the world as it is. This communicates that robotics can be viable in a narrower set of scenarios.

r003.rationale: The response describes recoverable mistakes such as a missed grasp, but does not identify lower safety risk as an advantage relative to self-driving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is both harder and easier, depending on the application. With self-driving, you have a pretty well-defined task and a very clear business case. The challenge is that you need an extremely high level of reliability in an environment you don’t control. You can’t really tell everyone else on the road how to behave.

With robotics, you have more flexibility in choosing the setting. You can start in a warehouse or a factory, constrain the task, and have a person step in when the robot gets stuck. That can make it easier to get something commercially useful before you’ve solved every edge case.

But manipulation is also really challenging. The robot has to make contact with the world, and small differences in an object’s shape or position can change what it needs to do. And there isn’t one obvious application that gives you the same scale of data and investment as driving.

So I think a lot comes down to finding tasks where the capabilities we have today are useful enough, and where deploying robots lets us collect the data to make them better.

r001.rationale: The response says manipulation is challenging because contact and small object differences affect actions, but it does not identify a higher-dimensional control space.

r002.rationale: It contrasts self-driving in an uncontrolled environment with robotics deployments in constrained settings such as warehouses or factories, where the task can be limited.

r003.rationale: The response mentions a person stepping in when a robot gets stuck, but does not identify lower safety risk as an advantage over self-driving.
